## Basics: {.unnumbered}

1. Import required functionS from the `math` library.
2. Assign a value to a variable using the assignment operator `=`
3. Perform a simple calculation and assign the result to a variable.
4. Print (display) the result in a formatted `f-string`.


## Functions {.unnumbered}

1. The inbuilt `round` function takes two arguments:  
(i) the number to round;  
(ii) the number of decimal places required.

1. Defining a new function stores it in memory for later use.  
Positional argumets must be given in the order specified.  
Keyword arguments use the `=` operator and take default values that are used if not specified when the function is called.
2. Any variable names used in the function definition are **not** seen by the main program and do not conflict with variables of the same name therein.
3. The `return` keyword passes any number of variables back as a result to the main program when the function is called later.  
Anything following the application of `return` in a function is ignored.
4. Variables passed as arguments to the function when it is applied do not need to have the same name as in the function definition, as the two are independent of each other.  
Keyword arguments can have the same name as the keyword itself without confusion, e.g.: `mean=mean` would work perfectly well if the word to the right of the `=` was a variable name.

## Conditionals {.unnumbered}

1. Putting other code elements in a function block allows reuse of code for efficiency.
2. `if` is a truth check that runs the code block if the condition (_"less than or equal to"_) is `True` and not if it is `False`. 
3. `elif` ("else if") is only considered when the first `if` was **not** satisfied.
4. `else` covers all other eventualities when none of the previous conditions were met.

## Iteration {.unnumbered}

1. A variable must exist for a conditional to work.
2. `while` is like `if` but the code-block _"loops"_ (repeats from the start of the block) until the condition is no longer true.
3. The variable tested against the condition must change or the loop will never exit!

## Lists and loops {.unnumbered}

1. The `range(N)` function counts `N` times (from $0$ to $N-1$).  
The `list` function turns a valid argument into a Python list.

1. New lists can be made using square brackets `[]` or generated from other lists using the `[OPERATION for ITEM in LISTNAME]` syntax. 

1. A `list` or other _"iterable"_  (such as the `range` function) can be iterated (_"looped"_) through using a `for` loop.  
In this example `n` successively takes each value in the range 0 to 10 (so 11 values in total).  
When looping through a list it would similarly take each value in that list in turn.
2. The block is executed for each item in the list.  
Note: here the value of `n` is actually used in the calculation, but it can also simply act as a counter for a fixed number of iterations.

## Example: Numerical Integration {.unnumbered}

Some functions such as the normal distribution $\displaystyle y = \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}$ cannot be integrated analytically (by hand).

We can do this numerically by approximating the area under the curve using finite blocks of width $\Delta x$ and height $y$ and adding their area. See the plots in [Section 6.](#6.-Plotting)

**The code below combines the programming building blocks above to approximate the area under (integrate) the normal distribution between two values $x=a$ and $x=b$**

1. The function can take either one or two arguments. The second one defaults to the special `None` datatype
2. If no second argument (with optional keyword `params`) is specified they take default values. 
3. The normal distribution is assumed standardised unless otherwise specified:  
$\mu = 0$, $\sigma = 1$
4. Specify the constant in the equation 
5. Normalisation for when this isn't already the case.
6. Calculate the Probability Distribution Function at the value of $x$.
7. Return the PDF value for use in the main function.
8. The first argument is the name of any function to be numerically integrated.
9. Define a variable that we will add successive elements of area to (see [the definition of integration](https://www.mathsisfun.com/calculus/integration-introduction.html) using small slices under a curve).
10. Take sucessive values of $x$, starting at the lower limit $a$.
11. Repeat the steps below until $x=a$.
12. Evaluate the height $y$ of the function $y=f(x)$ at each value of $x$ in turn in the loop.
13. Calculate the area of the current rectangular element 
14. Add the new element area to the total area
15. Increase $x$ to the next step along.
16. When $x>b$ the `while` loop exits and the function returns the numerical estimate of the area under the curve between $a\leq x\leq b$.
17. Integrate the normal distribution function between $-3\leq x\leq 3$ with a slice width $\Delta x = 0.1$.
18. Empty lists are defined to store data values in.
19. The Cumulative Distribution Function consists of values of the integral $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^b \operatorname{PDF}$ for different values of $b$.
20. Generate a list of $N$ values from `xmin` (when $i=0$) to `xmax` (when $i=20$).
21. For each of the 21 b-values to evaluate at.
22. Calculate the value of the normal distribution.
23. Integrate the normal distruibution to estimate the CDF at that point.  
**Note:** `normal(-10)` is close enough to zero, so we don't need to go to $-\infty$!
24. Append the function values for each of the PDF and CDF to their respective lists.

## Plotting {.unnumbered}

1. Import the plotting library
2. Generate a new figure canvas to plot graphs on
3. Make a layout that's one column and two rows of axes, the third argument says which axis to plot on for the `ax1` figure object.
4. Plot a bar graph with `bvals` on the $x-$axis and the PDF values on the $y-$axis, with bar widths matching the step-size in the previous code.
5. Set a new pair of plotting axes `ax2` for the second subplot. 
6. It's **not** good practice to use figure titles, better to label them (a) and (b) and discuss in the caption. Here for convenience only.
7. Save the figure as an image file to use in reports etc.

## Manipulating and analysing data {.unnumbered}
